tagline.text: A ridge hike among antenna towers above the clouds, 2,200 m-plus south of Baguio

location.label: Location
location.text: Tuba, Benguet; around Dontogan village (Green Valley) south of Baguio City

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300~1,500 (per person, based on transport from Baguio and snacks)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL; overland from Manila to Baguio)

children.text: Mount Santo Tomas in Tuba, Benguet, rises about 2,260 m, and a road reaches the summit, so it has been promoted as a half-day hike from Baguio. However, the Santo Tomas Forest Reserve has been closed to tourist entry by DENR under a court protection order (per 2016-2019 notices and reports; no reopening found), so check with DENR-CAR before you go. On a clear day you look down on Baguio, Lingayen Gulf and the high peaks of the Cordillera.

Mount Santo Tomas stands in the Tuba municipality of Benguet province, in the central part of the Cordillera range in northern Luzon. Wikipedia gives the summit elevation as about 2,260 m and its prominence as about 888 m. The hiking site Pinoy Mountaineer lists the same mountain at about 2,256 m and a road-guide site at about 2,224 m, so sources differ slightly; it is enough to think of it as "roughly the mid-2,200s." Looking south from downtown Baguio (about 1,500 m above sea level), the ridge lined with antennas is this mountain.

The mountain is a popular hiking goal because access is easy. Several telecom and broadcast relay stations stand around the summit, so a road runs up the ridge, and the hiking site describes it as one of the highest peaks in the Philippines you can reach by public transport. If you ride a jeepney or taxi from central Baguio to Green Valley and start walking, you can reach the area near the summit and return within half a day, and the climb is rated 2 out of 9 (a minor climb). Some people even ride mountain bikes up. It is a good alternative for anyone who finds a big trip like Mount Pulag, with its pre-dawn transfer and camping, too demanding.

Geologically, Mount Santo Tomas is a stratovolcano in the Luzon Volcanic Arc, classified by PHIVOLCS (the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology) as potentially active. Wikipedia records a last eruption on January 4, 1641, but the Global Volcanism Program regards its last activity as uncertain. The mountain lies within the Santo Tomas Forest Reserve, which President Quezon declared by Proclamation No. 581 in 1940, and in 2015 the Court of Appeals issued a Permanent Environment Protection Order (PEPO) that has restricted entry by tourists and non-residents (DENR-CAR reaffirmed the tourist ban in 2016, and in 2019 checkpoints were reported turning vehicles away). In other words, this is a protected forest and a mountain with communications facilities before it is a tourist site, so please leave no trash and follow the path and facility notices.

This guide is for travelers staying in Baguio who have half a day or a day to spare and want scenery different from the city sights. Strictly speaking, hiking Mount Santo Tomas is less about "conquering a single summit" and more about enjoying the whole route, passing the neighboring Mount Cabuyao ridge on the way to the summit ridge. Along the route you see vegetable terraces, small shops and a radar station, and in good weather you can look west over La Union and Lingayen Gulf. In the cloudy afternoon or the rainy season the view nearly disappears, so make weather and an early start the first priority when planning.

blocks.title: Mount Cabuyao radar station and vegetable terraces

children.text: Walking up from Green Valley, you reach Mount Cabuyao (about
) after roughly
5 km

. Two radar dishes stand there, which locals call "Ra-dar." The surrounding slopes are vegetable terraces growing potatoes and cabbages, and there are shops selling cold drinks and snacks, so it is a good place to rest.

blocks.title: The route from Mount Cabuyao to the summit ridge

children.text: From Mount Cabuyao to the summit of Mount Santo Tomas is about
4 km
, and guides say it takes roughly
1 to 1.5 hours
on foot. The road is wide and well established, and the steep part is only the last
20 minutes
or so. At the two junctions, you are told to turn right.

As you near the summit you pass at least four hills that look like "peaks." The highest has the most antenna towers, because telecom and broadcast companies built relay stations at this height. The facilities are closed to the public, so do not go inside the fences.
The summit is marked by a cross, said to have yellow and blue stained glass on its back. It is a good place for a commemorative photo, and on windy days you should wear an extra layer.

blocks.title: Views of Baguio and Lingayen Gulf

children.text: On a clear morning you look down on Baguio and surrounding towns, La Union to the west, and Lingayen Gulf opening to the South China Sea (West Philippine Sea) to the south. You can also pick out Baguio landmarks such as the Philippine Military Academy, Loakan Airport and SM City Baguio.

On a very clear day, four of the five highest mountains in the Philippines (Singakalsa, Tabayoc, Panotoan and Pulag) and Mount Ugo are said to be visible to the east. Clouds rise early here, so this view is sharpest before

Wild raspberries that locals call "sampinit" grow along the trail. One hiker wrote that he climbed without breakfast and eased his hunger with these berries. Since there are times when the fruit is not available, it is safer to bring your own snacks.
If walking is hard, you can also drive up near the summit. A road starts from 208 Road south of Baguio and climbs about
; it is narrow and steep. In places the grade reaches up to about
20 percent
and one side is a cliff, so if you are not confident driving it, use a local driver.

items.title: Half-day hike
items.subtitle: Round trip from Green Valley to the summit

children.text: From central Baguio, take a jeepney or taxi toward Marcos Highway to Green Valley (Dontogan village).
Arrive at Green Valley and start walking. Follow the rough road toward Mount Cabuyao. There are shortcuts, but if there are no signs, stay on the main road.
Reach the Mount Cabuyao radar area, take photos and catch your breath with a snack.
Head for the summit. At the two junctions, take the right-hand road.
Reach the summit of Mount Santo Tomas (the cross), enjoy the view and have a snack.
Go down the same way. The sun is climbing by now, so check your hat and sunscreen.
Return to the Green Valley trailhead and travel to Baguio for a late lunch.
These times are based on the schedule from a hiking guide site. They vary with your pace and rest stops, so leave some margin.

items.title: Pre-dawn route
items.subtitle: Climb in the dark to see sunrise and city lights

children.text: Take a taxi to the foot of Mount Cabuyao, or turn on a headlamp and start walking from Green Valley. One blogger wrote that a taxi from his hotel to the Mount Cabuyao station cost ₱600 (as of 2012).
Clouds and fog can be thick at dawn. Climb slowly and enjoy the time when you can see the moon and the lights of Baguio.
After sunrise the fog lifts and the terraces and distant ridges appear. The view is said to get better on the way down.
Have breakfast near the summit and start down before the clouds rise.
Mountain paths in the dark are easy to lose and chilly, so go with a group rather than alone and bring a headlamp and a power bank.

If you start from Manila, first travel to Baguio. Long-distance buses run from Manila and Clark to Baguio, and the travel time and fare vary greatly with the bus company, season and traffic, so check when you book.
The easiest plan is to check into a hotel in Baguio and climb early the next morning. For Baguio itself, see
Baguio
Overland travel can jam heavily on holidays and weekends, so leave extra time.

According to Pinoy Mountaineer, from central Baguio you take a jeepney or taxi heading toward Marcos Highway to Green Valley (Dontogan). The jeepney fare given there is ₱12.50, but that is old information, so confirm locally.
If you take a taxi, first check whether the meter will be used or agree on a price. A taxi is easier if you have luggage or a group.
There is a paved road of about
climbing from 208 Road to the summit. The average grade is about 6 percent, up to about 20 percent in places, and it is narrow with a cliff on one side.
If you use a private vehicle or a local driver, check road conditions and weather first, and avoid driving on rainy days or in thick fog.
Once up the mountain you mostly move on foot. The road is wide, so it is unlikely you will get lost, but on foggy days check the right-hand turn at every junction.
The hiking guide site says the best time to visit this mountain is the dry (summer) season. There is almost no shade along the route, so the midday sun is strong and sunscreen and a hat are needed.
The best time of day is early morning. Clouds often rise from late morning and the view turns hazy in the afternoon. In the rainy season or after rain, the road is muddy and the view is blocked.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: Cold at dawn and windy on the ridge; the best views of the year
Strong midday sun, so walk early in the morning
Slippery trail and poor visibility; avoid rainy days

There is no organized guidance on staying overnight on the mountain. Most people start from a hotel in central Baguio and return the same day. To leave early, a hotel near Marcos Highway or in the city center is convenient. For the city center, see
Session Road

Near Mount Cabuyao on the mountain there are shops selling cold drinks and snacks, and fresh strawberries are said to be sold too. Still, do not expect a proper restaurant, so prepare water, snacks and a packed lunch. After the descent, a late lunch in central Baguio works well. It is a protected reserve, so do not camp without permission and check the rules first.
Plan to start before dawn or early in the morning. Clouds rise early and the afternoon view can turn hazy.
There is almost no shade. Bring a hat, sunglasses and sunscreen.
Some sections are rocky, so hiking shoes are safer than sneakers.
Bring water, snacks and a packed lunch. The shops on the mountain are small and sometimes closed.
Mobile phone signal is said to be good along most of the route. Still, bring a power bank and an offline map.
The antennas and relay stations are restricted facilities. Do not go inside fences and be careful about photographing them.
Carry out all trash. Because this is a forest reserve, do not light fires or pick plants.
If you are planning Mount Pulag, try this mountain as an easy practice hike.

This mountain is a forest reserve, and DENR-CAR has barred tourist entry under a court protection order, running checkpoints with the police (per 2016-2019 notices and reports; no recent reopening found). Without approval you may be turned back, so check with DENR-CAR or the Tuba municipal office first. The summit road is narrow with a steep cliff on one side. Rain or fog makes both driving and walking dangerous, so postpone your trip on bad-weather days.

Trail conditions and hiking schedules here come mainly from 2012–2015 hiking guides and are dated; unlike then, entry restrictions may now apply. Before you go, check the latest situation with DENR-CAR, the Tuba municipal office or the Baguio tourism office.
On a shadeless ridge there is a risk of heatstroke and dehydration at midday. Drink plenty of water.
Areas with telecom and broadcast facilities are restricted. Follow signs and the instructions of security staff.
Mount Santo Tomas is classified by PHIVOLCS as a potentially active volcano. The everyday risk is not large, but avoid hiking when there is news of earthquakes or landslides.
If you hike alone before dawn, tell your family or hotel your plans.
The first city you reach after coming down the mountain,
Baguio
is a good place to end the day with its market, cafes and parks.
A park with an artificial lake in the middle of Baguio; at
Burnham Park
you can ride a boat or stroll to loosen your legs.
A resort complex surrounded by pine forest; at
Camp John Hay
you can have a relaxed meal or a walk.
A strawberry farm in La Trinidad, Benguet; at
La Trinidad Strawberry Farm
you can pick strawberries and buy souvenirs.
If gazing at the Cordillera peaks from Santo Tomas has stirred you,
Mount Pulag
is the next destination.
